steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting MatchXML, a framework for extreme multi-label text classification. Introduce the problem and its applications, explain our label-embedding and text-representation ideas against prior work, and end with an outline of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- XMC problem and applications
- Hierarchical label trees and PIFA label embeddings; their limitations
- label2vec: dense label embeddings via Skip-gram
- Text representations: sparse vs dense; our text-label matching fine-tuning and Sentence-T5 embeddings
- Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- XMC
  - classifier annotating input text with most relevant labels from extremely large label set (e.g., millions)
  - applications: Wikipedia page tags (cite), customer query -> products in product search (cite), recommending items in recommendation systems (cite)
- HLT and PIFA
  - Hierarchical Label Tree (HLT) (cite): complexity O(L) -> O(logL), L = number of labels
  - built from label embeddings by partition algorithms (cite) based on K-means clustering
  - prior works (cite) use Positive Instance Feature Aggregation (PIFA): label embedding = sum of TF–IDF features of samples where label positive
  - limitations: (1) ML algorithms more efficient on small dense vectors than large sparse vectors; (2) TF–IDF features not always available -> limits PIFA
- label2vec
  - inspired by word2vec (cite) word embeddings
  - label set of a sample = unordered sequence, each label a word/token; Skip-gram model (cite) trains label embeddings
  - better generalization than PIFA (no TF–IDF needed); smaller storage, more efficient downstream
  - experiments: captures semantic label relationships, improved HLTs vs sparse embeddings -> better XMC
- Text representations
  - early XMC works (cite, many): statistical BOW or TF–IDF features to train classifier; simple, but ignore word order -> no semantics
  - recent works (cite): deep learning dense vectors using contextual information -> better accuracy
  - XR-Transformer (cite), CascadeXML (cite): sparse TF–IDF and dense features not mutually exclusive, use together
  - ours: combine both; novel method to improve dense features
  - fine-tuning pre-trained encoder Transformer: multi-label classification as text-label matching in bipartite graph; text-label + label-text alignment -> robust dense text representations
  - also static dense sentence embeddings from pre-trained Sentence Transformers (text classification, clustering, retrieval, paraphrase detection); capture semantics vs sparse TF-IDF
  - Sentence-T5 (cite) embeddings integrated into MatchXML; very effective in ablation study
- Organization
  - II related work: extreme classification, cross-modal learning, contrastive learning
  - III MatchXML: label2vec, hierarchical label tree, text-label matching, linear ranker
  - IV experiments on six benchmark datasets, comparisons
  - V conclusions and future work

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
eXtreme Multi-label text Classification (XMC) means learning a classifier that annotates an input text with the most relevant labels out of an extremely large label set (for example, millions of labels). The problem has many real world applications, like labeling a Wikipedia page with relevant tags, giving a customer query the related products in product search, and recommending relevant items to a customer in recommendation systems.

The output space in XMC is extremely large, and to handle it the Hierarchical Label Tree (HLT) was proposed, which reduces the computational complexity from O(L) to O(logL), where L is the number of labels. An HLT takes label embeddings as input and can be built by partition algorithms based on K-means clustering. Prior works used Positive Instance Feature Aggregation (PIFA) to compute the label embeddings, where a label embedding is the sum of the TF–IDF features of the text samples where the label is positive. But label embeddings from PIFA have several limitations. First, current machine learning algorithms process small dense vectors more efficiently than large sparse vectors. Second, PIFA needs the TF–IDF features of the text data to generate the label embeddings, and these may not always be available, which limits where PIFA can be used. Inspired by word2vec for training word embeddings, we propose label2vec to learn semantic dense label embeddings. We treat the set of labels assigned to a text sample as an unordered sequence, where each label is like one word/token, and we apply the Skip-gram model to train an embedding for each label. label2vec generalizes better than PIFA because it does not need the TF–IDF features. Also the dense label embeddings take less storage and are more efficient for the downstream machine learning algorithms to process. Our experiments show that the dense label embeddings capture semantic label relationships and give better HLTs than the sparse label embeddings, which leads to better performance in the downstream XMC tasks.

- Text representations
  - early XMC: statistical BOW / TF–IDF features; simple but ignore word order -> no semantic meaning
  - recent works: deep learning dense vectors from contextual information -> better accuracy
  - XR-Transformer, CascadeXML: sparse and dense not mutually exclusive, use together
  - ours: combine both + new method for better dense features: fine-tune pre-trained encoder Transformer as text-label matching in bipartite graph (text-label and label-text alignment)
  - plus static dense sentence embeddings from pre-trained Sentence Transformers; Sentence-T5 integrated into MatchXML; effective in ablation
- Organization: II related work (extreme classification, cross-modal, contrastive); III MatchXML components (label2vec, HLT, text-label matching, linear ranker); IV six benchmark datasets; V conclusions, future work

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
eXtreme Multi-label text Classification (XMC) means learning a classifier that annotates an input text with the most relevant labels out of an extremely large label set (for example, millions of labels). The problem has many real world applications, like labeling a Wikipedia page with relevant tags, giving a customer query the related products in product search, and recommending relevant items to a customer in recommendation systems.

The output space in XMC is extremely large, and to handle it the Hierarchical Label Tree (HLT) was proposed, which reduces the computational complexity from O(L) to O(logL), where L is the number of labels. An HLT takes label embeddings as input and can be built by partition algorithms based on K-means clustering. Prior works used Positive Instance Feature Aggregation (PIFA) to compute the label embeddings, where a label embedding is the sum of the TF–IDF features of the text samples where the label is positive. But label embeddings from PIFA have several limitations. First, current machine learning algorithms process small dense vectors more efficiently than large sparse vectors. Second, PIFA needs the TF–IDF features of the text data to generate the label embeddings, and these may not always be available, which limits where PIFA can be used. Inspired by word2vec for training word embeddings, we propose label2vec to learn semantic dense label embeddings. We treat the set of labels assigned to a text sample as an unordered sequence, where each label is like one word/token, and we apply the Skip-gram model to train an embedding for each label. label2vec generalizes better than PIFA because it does not need the TF–IDF features. Also the dense label embeddings take less storage and are more efficient for the downstream machine learning algorithms to process. Our experiments show that the dense label embeddings capture semantic label relationships and give better HLTs than the sparse label embeddings, which leads to better performance in the downstream XMC tasks.

Most early XMC works use the statistical Bag-Of-Words (BOW) or Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF–IDF) features as text representations to train a text classifier. These features are simple, but they ignore word order, so they can not capture the semantic meaning of text corpora. Recent works use deep learning approaches to learn dense vectors as text representations. These methods use the contextual information of words in the text corpora to get dense text representations, and this improves classification accuracy. On the other hand, the recently proposed XR-Transformer and CascadeXML showed that sparse TF–IDF features and dense text features are not mutually exclusive, and they can be used together as text representations to boost performance. Following this strategy, we build the final text representations from both sparse TF–IDF features and dense vector features, and we propose a new method to improve the quality of the dense vector features for XMC. In the fine-tuning stage of the pre-trained encoder Transformer, we formulate multi-label text classification as a text-label matching problem in a bipartite graph. With text-label alignment and label-text alignment in the bipartite graph, the fine-tuned Transformer gives robust and effective dense text representations. Besides these fine-tuned dense text representations, we also use static dense sentence embeddings extracted from pre-trained Sentence Transformers, which are widely used in NLP for tasks like text classification, clustering, retrieval, and paraphrase detection. The static dense sentence embeddings can capture semantic meaning, unlike the sparse TF-IDF representations, and help the downstream applications. Specifically, we extract static sentence embeddings from Sentence-T5 and integrate them into MatchXML. We found this approach to be very effective, as our ablation study shows.

The rest of the paper is organized like this. In Section II we review related works on extreme classification, cross-modal learning and contrastive learning. Section III presents the proposed method MatchXML and introduces its main components, which are label2vec, the hierarchical label tree, text-label matching, and the linear ranker. Section IV presents experimental results on six benchmark datasets, with comparisons to other algorithms in the literature. Section V discusses conclusions and future work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The eXtreme Multi-label text Classification (XMC) refers to learning a classifier that can annotate an input text with the most relevant labels from an extremely large-scale label set (e.g., millions of labels). This problem has many real world applications, such as labeling a Wikipedia page with relevant tags [1], providing a customer query with related products in product search [2], and recommending relevant items to a customer in recommendation systems [3].

To address the extremely large output space in XMC, the Hierarchical Label Tree (HLT) [2] has been proposed to reduce the computational complexity from O(L) to O(logL), where L is the number of labels. Taking label embeddings as input, an HLT can be constructed by partition algorithms [2,4] based on K-means clustering. Prior works [2,4,5,6,7] have applied the Positive Instance Feature Aggregation (PIFA) to compute label embeddings, where one label embedding is the summation of the TF–IDF features of the text samples when the label is positive. However, the label embeddings generated from PIFA have several limitations. First, current machine learning algorithms process small dense vectors more efficiently than large sparse vectors. Second, the TF–IDF features of text data, which PIFA requires to generate the label embeddings, may not always be available, which limits the applications of PIFA. Inspired by word2vec [8,9] for training word embeddings, we propose label2vec to learn semantic dense label embeddings. We consider the set of labels assigned to a text sample as an unordered sequence, where each label is treated as one word/token, and apply the Skip-gram model [8,9] to train the embedding for each label. label2vec has better generalization than PIFA as it does not require the TF–IDF features. Besides, the dense label embeddings have a smaller storage size and are more efficient for downstream machine learning algorithms to process. Our experiments demonstrate that the dense label embeddings can capture semantic label relationships and generate improved HLTs compared to the sparse label embeddings, leading to improved performance in the downstream XMC tasks.

Most of the early works in XMC [10,11,12,13,14,15,16,2,17,18,19,20,21,22] leverage the statistical Bag-Of-Words (BOW) or Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF–IDF) features as text representations to train a text classifier. These features are simple, but they can not capture the semantic meaning of text corpora because they ignore word order. Recent works [23,24,6,25,5] explore deep learning approaches to learn dense vectors as text representations. These methods leverage the contextual information of words in text corpora to extract dense text representations, leading to improved classification accuracies. On the other hand, the recently proposed XR-Transformer [7] and CascadeXML [26] have shown that sparse TF–IDF features and dense text features are not mutually exclusive, but can be leveraged together as text representations to boost performance. Inspired by this strategy, we generate the final text representations by taking advantage of both sparse TF–IDF features and dense vector features, and we propose a novel method to improve the quality of the dense vector features for XMC. Specifically, in the fine-tuning stage of the pre-trained encoder Transformer, we formulate multi-label text classification as a text-label matching problem in a bipartite graph. Through text-label alignment and label-text alignment in the bipartite graph, the fine-tuned Transformer yields robust and effective dense text representations. Besides these fine-tuned dense text representations, we also utilize static dense sentence embeddings extracted from pre-trained Sentence Transformers, which are widely used in NLP for tasks such as text classification, clustering, retrieval, and paraphrase detection. Compared with sparse TF-IDF representations, static dense sentence embeddings can capture semantic meaning and facilitate downstream applications. In particular, we extract static sentence embeddings from Sentence-T5 [27] and integrate them into MatchXML. We have found this approach to be very effective, as shown in our ablation study.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we review related works from the perspectives of extreme classification, cross-modal learning and contrastive learning. The proposed method MatchXML is presented in Section III, where its main components, label2vec, the hierarchical label tree, text-label matching, and the linear ranker, are introduced. Experimental results on six benchmark datasets are presented in Section IV, with comparisons to other algorithms in the literature. Conclusions and future work are discussed in Section V.
